Q9036.L1t: Scars form as part of the normal healing process after skin is injured, and their appearance varies between individuals.
Q9036.L2t: Keloids tend to be more common in people with darker skin and often develop after surgery, burns or other skin injury.
Q9036.L3t: A keloid results from excessive collagen deposition that grows beyond the original wound edges, producing a raised, thick, dense area of tissue.
Q9036.L4t: A keloid is a firm, raised mass of scar tissue.
Q9036.L2f: Keloids occur almost exclusively in very young infants and never develop after surgical incisions.
Q9036.L3f: A keloid forms when too little collagen is laid down, so the healed wound remains flat, narrow and barely visible.
Q9036.L4f: A keloid is a fine, hairline scar.

Q9037.L1t: A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck into the windpipe, and it can be temporary or permanent.
Q9037.L2t: A tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway, and the tube placed in the opening may be cuffed or uncuffed depending on the patient's needs.
Q9037.L3t: A tracheostomy tube lets sedation be reduced and gives direct access to the airway, so ventilator support can be lowered in steps as breathing recovers.
Q9037.L4t: A tracheostomy can be used to help wean patients off a ventilator.
Q9037.L2f: A tracheostomy tube is always placed above the vocal cords, and it is inserted through the mouth rather than through the neck.
Q9037.L3f: A tracheostomy tube sits at the level of the larynx and acts as a support that restores vocal cord movement, so it directly treats the paralysed cords.
Q9037.L4f: A tracheostomy is done to repair the vocal cords after paralysis.

Q9038.L1t: Osteopathic manipulative treatment includes many techniques, such as articulatory, muscle energy and soft tissue methods, each with its own risks and contraindications.
Q9038.L2t: The vertebral arteries pass through the cervical transverse foramina and can be vulnerable to vertebrobasilar insufficiency, especially in older patients.
Q9038.L3t: Combined rotation and extension of the neck stretches and narrows the vertebral arteries, which can reduce blood flow to the brainstem and cause confusion, nausea and vertigo.
Q9038.L4t: The physician may be liable if the neck was treated in simultaneous hyperrotation and extension.
Q9038.L2f: Cervical manipulation affects only the paraspinal muscles, and the arteries of the neck are not mechanically affected by neck positioning.
Q9038.L3f: Osteoarthritis of the cervical spine is an absolute contraindication to any neck treatment, so treating such a patient at all is a clear breach of the standard of care.
Q9038.L4f: The physician may be liable if the patient was previously treated for osteoarthritis of the cervical spine.
